what_it_is.prose: Rolls-Royce plc is the United Kingdom's principal aero-engine and power-systems manufacturer, with civil aerospace, defence and power-systems businesses. Its India relationship is one of the oldest of any Western engine OEM and spans several in-service military powerplants. The Rolls-Royce AE 2100D3 turboprop (four per aircraft) powers the Indian Air Force's Lockheed Martin C-130J-30 Super Hercules special-operations/tactical airlifters; in August 2025 Rolls-Royce said it was 'exploring potential opportunities' to set up an MRO facility in India for the AE2100 engine operated by the IAF, and to scale the partnership toward assembly and testing for the wider Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) programme — framed against the India-UK CETA trade agreement and a plan to double India sourcing over five years. Separately, the Rolls-Royce Turbomeca Adour (Mk 811/821/871) powers India's SEPECAT Jaguar strike fighters and BAE Hawk advanced jet trainers — the IAF operates among the world's largest serving fleets of both. In September 2021 Rolls-Royce and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) signed a pact under which HAL manufactures Adour engine spare parts for Rolls-Royce's global defence customer base and hosts an Authorized Maintenance Centre for the Adour, building on HAL's 30-plus years of Adour licence production and support. Rolls-Royce also markets naval power (MT30) and is a candidate powerplant partner for India's future fighter-engine ambitions. This dossier is scoped Tier B: genuine, multi-programme India relevance, but with limited public disclosure on contract values and quantities and an MRO plan still at an early stage.

deployments_procurement.summary: Rolls-Royce engines are embedded across three IAF fleets — the AE 2100D3 on the C-130J-30, and the Adour on the Jaguar and Hawk. India value-add is concentrated in HAL: licence production/support of the Adour and, since 2021, manufacture of Adour parts for Rolls-Royce's global customer base plus an Authorized Maintenance Centre. The AE2100 India MRO is at the exploratory stage (Aug 2025), and Rolls-Royce has positioned itself for the MTA programme's assembly/testing work.

open_questions: No public contract value or timeline for the planned AE2100 India MRO facility
Scope and volume of HAL-made Adour parts for Rolls-Royce's global base not publicly quantified

import_dependencies.summary: Rolls-Royce engines in Indian service are foreign-designed; India's value-add is confined to HAL licence assembly/MRO of the Adour and (planned) AE2100 overhaul. Core engine design authority, hot-section technology, single-crystal turbine blades and FADEC remain with Rolls-Royce in the UK, so the AE 2100 and Adour represent import-dependent propulsion on otherwise India-operated fleets.

faq.question: Which Indian military aircraft use Rolls-Royce engines?
faq.answer: The Rolls-Royce AE 2100D3 turboprop (four per aircraft) powers the Indian Air Force's C-130J-30 Super Hercules. The Rolls-Royce Turbomeca Adour (Mk 811/821/871) powers the IAF's SEPECAT Jaguar strike fighters and BAE Hawk advanced jet trainers, both among the largest serving fleets of their type in the world.

faq.question: Is Rolls-Royce setting up engine MRO in India?
faq.answer: Rolls-Royce announced in August 2025 that it is exploring an India MRO facility for the AE2100 engine operated by the IAF, and wants to scale the partnership toward assembly and testing for the Medium Transport Aircraft programme, aligned with the India-UK CETA agreement. It also plans to double its India sourcing over five years. Separately, since 2021 HAL runs an Authorized Maintenance Centre for the Adour and makes Adour parts for Rolls-Royce's global fleet.

faq.question: What is the Rolls-Royce–HAL partnership?
faq.answer: In September 2021, at Aero India, Rolls-Royce and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited signed a pact under which HAL manufactures Adour engine spare parts for Rolls-Royce's international defence customer base and hosts an Authorized Maintenance Centre for the Adour. HAL has over 30 years of experience supporting Adour engines in India, and Rolls-Royce described HAL as the first supplier in a wider Indian supply-chain ecosystem.
